ruleset.name: pmd-kotlin-preview
ruleset.description: PREVIEW of PMD's own Kotlin rules, TEMPORARY. Copied from the XPath rules in https://github.com/stokpop/pmd/tree/feature/kotlin-type-mapper (pmd-kotlin/src/main/resources/category/kotlin), so they can be tried out on a stock PMD without that build. Requires PMD 7.28.0 or newer (Kotlin type resolution XPath functions typeIs, typeIsExactly, matchesSig, isNullable) and the project classes/dependencies on the aux classpath. NOT included: rules implemented as Java classes (CognitiveComplexity, CyclomaticComplexity, ExcessiveParameterList, LocalVariableShadowsParameter, OverrideBothEqualsAndHashcode, ...) and rules using the fork-only XPath functions pmd-kotlin:nodeText() and pmd-kotlin:insideLoop(), and rules that rely on fork-only AST attributes (e.g. @Identifier on CatchBlock/PrimaryExpression) or Kotlin signature resolution not in 7.28.0 (their tests fail on stock PMD): PreserveStackTrace, UseStringBuilderLength, UselessStringValueOf, InefficientEmptyStringCheck, UseLocaleWithCaseConversions, UnnecessaryCaseChange, AvoidRethrowingException. Remove this file once these rules ship with PMD itself.

rule.name: AvoidMessageDigestField
rule.message: MessageDigest fields are not thread-safe; declare a local instance instead.
rule.description:
`java.security.MessageDigest` is not thread-safe. Declaring it as a class field exposes it to concurrent access without explicit synchronisation, producing incorrect digests. Create a new instance per method call, or protect shared access with a mutex.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/bestpractices.xml/AvoidMessageDigestField

rule.name: AvoidPrintStackTrace
rule.message: Avoid printStackTrace(); use kotlin-logging or a SLF4J logger instead.
rule.description:
Avoid calling `Throwable.printStackTrace()`; use a proper logger instead. Stack traces printed to standard output can be lost in production and carry no log level, making them hard to control or suppress.
Kotlin idiomatic alternative: use kotlin-logging (`io.github.microutils:kotlin-logging`): - `private val log = KotlinLogging.logger {}` - `log.error(e) { "operation failed" }`
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/bestpractices.xml/AvoidPrintStackTrace

rule.name: AvoidStringBufferField
rule.message: StringBuffer/StringBuilder fields can grow large; prefer buildString'{'...'}'or a local instance.
rule.description:
`StringBuffer` and `StringBuilder` instances can grow considerably and, if held as class fields across long-lived objects, may cause memory leaks.
Kotlin idiomatic alternatives: - Use `buildString { append(...) }` for one-shot construction (returns a `String` directly). - Create a local `StringBuilder` inside the function that needs it. - Prefer string templates (`"$var"`) which the Kotlin compiler optimises automatically.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/bestpractices.xml/AvoidStringBufferField

rule.name: FunctionNameTooShort
rule.message: Function names should have non-cryptic and clear names.
rule.description: Function names should be easy to understand and describe the intention. Makes developers happy. Short names that are conventional in Kotlin or platform idioms (e.g. event listener `on`, Android density-pixel helper `dp`) can be excluded via the `allowedNames` property.

property.name: allowedNames
property.description: Short function names that are conventional and should not be flagged.

rule.example:
fun cl() {} // violation
fun calculateLayout() {} // no violation
fun on(listener: () -> Unit) {} // no violation -- 'on' is in allowedNames by default
override fun on(event: String) {} // no violation -- overrides are always excluded
fun dp(value: Int): Int = (value * 2.5f).toInt() // no violation -- 'dp' is in allowedNames by default (Android convention)

rule.name: LooseCoupling
rule.message: Use the interface type (List/Set/Map) instead of a concrete implementation type as the declared type.
rule.description:
Declaring fields or properties with a concrete collection type (`ArrayList`, `HashSet`, `HashMap`, etc.) tightly couples callers to an implementation detail. Declare the type as the appropriate interface (`List`, `Set`, `Map`, `MutableList`, `MutableSet`, `MutableMap`) so the implementation can be swapped without breaking API consumers.
In Kotlin, prefer the idiomatic factory functions: - `listOf()` / `mutableListOf()` -> returns `MutableList` - `setOf()` / `mutableSetOf()` -> returns `MutableSet` - `mapOf()` / `mutableMapOf()` -> returns `MutableMap`
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/bestpractices.xml/LooseCoupling

rule.name: SystemPrintln
rule.message: Usage of System.out/err; use kotlin-logging or another logging framework.
rule.description:
Calls to `System.out.print*`, `System.err.print*`, or `System.out.printf` are typically left-over debug statements. Use a structured logging framework so output can be controlled by log level and configuration without redeploying.
Kotlin idiomatic alternative: kotlin-logging (`io.github.microutils:kotlin-logging`): - `private val log = KotlinLogging.logger {}` - `log.info { "message" }`
Note: Kotlin's built-in top-level `println()` also maps to `System.out` and should be replaced in production code. This rule detects the explicit `System.out/err` variants; treat `println()` / `print()` calls as violations in code review.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/bestpractices.xml/SystemPrintln

rule.name: AvoidBranchingStatementAsLastInLoop
rule.message: Branching statement directly in loop body without conditional guard makes the loop execute only once.
rule.description: Using a `break`, `continue`, or `return` directly in the body of a loop (not guarded by an `if` or `when`) causes the loop to execute at most once. This is almost always a bug or confusing code. Wrap the branching statement inside a conditional to make the intent explicit.

rule.name: AvoidCallingFinalize
rule.message: Do not call finalize() explicitly; rely on the garbage collector.
rule.description:
`finalize()` is called by the garbage collector automatically; calling it explicitly bypasses GC timing and can cause objects to be finalized twice. In Kotlin prefer `AutoCloseable` / `use {}` for resource cleanup.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/errorprone.xml/AvoidCallingFinalize

rule.name: AvoidCatchingGenericException
rule.message: Avoid catching overly broad exception types; catch specific exceptions instead.
rule.description:
Catching `Exception` or `RuntimeException` hides real error types and makes error handling imprecise. In Kotlin prefer `runCatching {}` with `.onFailure {}`, or catch specific exceptions.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/errorprone.xml/AvoidCatchingGenericException

rule.name: AvoidCatchingNPE
rule.message: Avoid catching NullPointerException; use Kotlin null-safety (?., ?:, !!) instead.
rule.description:
Catching `NullPointerException` is a code smell in Kotlin. Kotlin's type system distinguishes nullable from non-nullable types at compile time, making explicit NPE catches unnecessary and masking real bugs.
Kotlin idiomatic alternatives: - Use nullable types (`String?`) and safe calls (`str?.length ?: 0`) - Use the Elvis operator (`?:`) for default values - Use `requireNotNull()` or `checkNotNull()` for early validation
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/errorprone.xml/AvoidCatchingNPE

property.description: Java rule this Kotlin rule is based on; update this rule when the Java rule changes.

rule.name: AvoidCatchingThrowable
rule.message: Avoid catching Throwable; it includes Errors that should not be caught.
rule.description:
`Throwable` is the root of both `Exception` and `Error`. Catching it can swallow `OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError` and other JVM errors that are not recoverable. Catch specific exceptions instead. For result-oriented error handling prefer `runCatching {}` with `.onFailure {}`, which limits handling to non-fatal exceptions.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/errorprone.xml/AvoidCatchingThrowable

rule.name: AvoidDecimalFormatAsField
rule.message: Avoid using DecimalFormat or ChoiceFormat as a field: they are thread-unsafe.
rule.description: `DecimalFormat` and `ChoiceFormat` are thread-unsafe. Declaring them as fields introduces race conditions. Create a new instance per method call, or use a `ThreadLocal`.

rule.name: AvoidDecimalLiteralsInBigDecimalConstructor
rule.message: Avoid creating BigDecimal with a float/double literal; use a String literal instead.
rule.description:
`BigDecimal(0.1)` does not equal `0.1` exactly due to floating-point representation. Use `BigDecimal("0.1")`, `BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)`, or the Kotlin idiomatic `"0.1".toBigDecimal()` extension for exact decimal values.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/errorprone.xml/AvoidDecimalLiteralsInBigDecimalConstructor

property.name: javaEquivalentRule
property.description: Java rule this Kotlin rule is based on; update this rule when the Java rule changes.

rule.name: AvoidThrowingNullPointerException
rule.message: Avoid throwing NullPointerException; use requireNotNull() or checkNotNull() instead.
rule.description: Explicitly throwing `NullPointerException` is misleading -- callers and tools expect NPE to indicate an unintentional null dereference, not a deliberate contract violation. Use `requireNotNull()`, `checkNotNull()`, or `error()` to signal intentional null checks with a clear message.

rule.name: AvoidThrowingRawExceptionTypes
rule.message: Avoid throwing raw exception types; use a more specific exception subclass.
rule.description: Throwing generic root types (`Throwable`, `Error`, `Exception`, `RuntimeException`) loses semantic information. Callers cannot catch the specific condition without catching everything. Use a specific subclass that communicates the failure reason, or define a custom exception.

rule.name: DoNotExtendJavaLangError
rule.message: Do not extend Error or its standard subclasses; extend Exception or RuntimeException instead.
rule.description:
`java.lang.Error` and its subclasses (`AssertionError`, `LinkageError`, `VirtualMachineError`, `ThreadDeath`) represent serious JVM-level problems that application code should not model. Extending them creates custom error types that callers will not catch, since `catch(e: Exception)` does not catch `Error`.
Use `Exception` or `RuntimeException` (or a Kotlin sealed class hierarchy) instead.

rule.name: DoNotTerminateVM
rule.message: Avoid calling System.exit() or Runtime.halt(); throw an exception or use a proper shutdown hook instead.
rule.description:
Calling `System.exit()` or `Runtime.halt()` terminates the JVM abruptly, bypassing shutdown hooks, resource cleanup, and normal exception handling. In library code this is especially harmful as it kills the entire host process.
Prefer throwing an appropriate exception, or for application entry points register a shutdown hook via `Runtime.addShutdownHook()` and signal shutdown through a flag or coroutine cancellation.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/errorprone.xml/DoNotTerminateVM

property.name: javaEquivalentRule
property.description: Java rule this Kotlin rule is based on; update this rule when the Java rule changes.

rule.name: ReplaceJavaUtilDate
rule.message: Avoid using java.util.Date; use java.time API instead
rule.description: The legacy `java.util.Date` class is mutable, not thread-safe, and has a confusing API. Use the `java.time` API instead: `LocalDate` (date only), `LocalTime` (time only), `LocalDateTime` (date and time), `Instant` (timestamp), or `ZonedDateTime` (with timezone).

rule.name: ReturnFromFinallyBlock
rule.message: Avoid returning from a finally block; this can discard exceptions
rule.description: Avoid returning from a `finally` block. Returning from a `finally` block silently discards any exception that was thrown in the corresponding `try` or `catch` block, making bugs very hard to find.

rule.name: SimpleDateFormatNeedsLocale
rule.message: Specify a Locale when constructing a SimpleDateFormat
rule.description: Be sure to specify a `Locale` when creating `SimpleDateFormat` instances to ensure that locale-appropriate formatting is used. Without a locale, the default system locale is used which can cause unexpected results in internationalized applications. Prefer `java.time` APIs (such as `DateTimeFormatter`) which have explicit locale support.

rule.name: UnresolvedType
rule.message: Type ''{0}'' could not be resolved -- add the missing dependency to the PMD analysis classpath for full type-aware analysis.
rule.description:
Reports import declarations whose type could not be resolved by the `kotlin-type-mapper` pre-analysis step. This typically means that a library or SDK dependency is not on the PMD analysis classpath.
When types are unresolved, type-aware rules (such as `UseStringBuilderForStringAppends`, `UseLocaleWithCaseConversions`, and `ReplaceJavaUtilDate`) may miss violations or report false positives for code that uses those types.
To fix: pass the missing JARs via the PMD `--classpath` option (or the `auxclasspath` configuration in your build plugin) so the type mapper can resolve all referenced types.

rule.name: DontCallThreadRun
rule.message: Don't call Thread.run() explicitly; call Thread.start() to execute in a new thread. Consider using coroutines instead.
rule.description:
Calling `thread.run()` executes the `run()` method in the current thread, not a new one. Use `thread.start()` to actually create a new thread. For Kotlin prefer coroutines (`launch {}`) over raw threads.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/multithreading.xml/DontCallThreadRun

rule.name: UseConcurrentHashMap
rule.message: Use ConcurrentHashMap instead of HashMap for concurrent access. Consider using a coroutine-safe data structure.
rule.description:
`HashMap` is not thread-safe. In multi-threaded code, concurrent reads/writes without synchronization can corrupt the map. Use `ConcurrentHashMap` for safe concurrent access, or consider Kotlin coroutine-friendly alternatives.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/multithreading.xml/UseConcurrentHashMap

rule.name: UseNotifyAllInsteadOfNotify
rule.message: Call notifyAll() rather than notify() to wake all waiting threads. Consider using coroutines instead.
rule.description:
`notify()` wakes only one thread waiting on an object's monitor, chosen arbitrarily. `notifyAll()` wakes all waiting threads and avoids missed wake-up bugs. For Kotlin prefer coroutine primitives (`Mutex`, `Channel`, `StateFlow`) over raw synchronization.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/multithreading.xml/UseNotifyAllInsteadOfNotify

rule.name: AvoidArrayLoops
rule.message: Use copyInto() or copyOf() instead of manually copying array elements in a loop.
rule.description:
Manually copying array elements one by one in a loop is less efficient and less clear than using the built-in `copyInto()` or `copyOf()` functions. The built-in functions are implemented natively and avoid the overhead of interpreted looping.
Prefer: - `src.copyInto(dst)` for a full copy into an existing array - `src.copyOf()` or `src.copyOf(n)` to produce a new copy - `src.copyOfRange(from, to)` for a partial copy
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/performance.xml/AvoidArrayLoops

rule.name: AvoidCalendarDateCreation
rule.message: Avoid creating Calendar instances; use the java.time API (LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime) instead.
rule.description:
`java.util.Calendar` is a heavyweight, mutable object. Creating a `Calendar` instance just to obtain the current date or time is expensive and unnecessarily verbose.
Prefer the modern `java.time` API introduced in Java 8: - `java.time.LocalDateTime.now()` / `ZonedDateTime.now()` for date-time values - `java.time.Instant.now()` for a machine timestamp - `java.time.LocalDate.today()` for date-only values
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/performance.xml/AvoidCalendarDateCreation

rule.name: AvoidCallingGcExplicitly
rule.message: Avoid explicit garbage-collection calls; the JVM manages memory automatically.
rule.description:
Calling `System.gc()` or `Runtime.getRuntime().gc()` requests a GC cycle but does not guarantee one will run. In practice it introduces unpredictable pauses and can degrade throughput. The JVM's garbage collector is designed to manage memory automatically; manual invocations are almost never correct.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/performance.xml/AvoidCallingGcExplicitly

rule.name: AvoidFileStream
rule.message: Avoid FileInputStream/FileOutputStream/FileReader/FileWriter; use File.inputStream() or Files.newInputStream().
rule.description:
`FileInputStream`/`OutputStream`/`Reader`/`Writer` contain a finalizer that can cause GC pressure. In Kotlin prefer: - `File.inputStream()` / `File.outputStream()` for byte streams - `File.bufferedReader()` / `File.bufferedWriter()` for character streams - `File.readBytes()` / `File.readText()` / `File.writeText()` for one-shot reads/writes - `Files.newInputStream(path)` / `Files.newOutputStream(path)` for the NIO2 approach All of these avoid the finalizer and work naturally with `use {}`.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/performance.xml/AvoidFileStream

rule.name: InefficientStringBuffering
rule.message: Avoid concatenating non-literals in a StringBuilder.append() call; use chained append() calls instead.
rule.description:
Passing a `+` concatenation expression to `StringBuilder.append()` or `StringBuffer.append()` creates an intermediate `String` object unnecessarily. Use chained `append()` calls or Kotlin's `buildString { }` builder instead.
Kotlin idiomatic alternatives: - Chain: `sb.append("prefix").append(variable)` - Builder: `buildString { append("prefix"); append(variable) }`
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/performance.xml/InefficientStringBuffering

rule.name: StringInstantiation
rule.message: Avoid creating String objects unnecessarily; use a String literal instead.
rule.description:
Strings are immutable in Kotlin/JVM. Creating `String(someString)` just copies the reference to a new object; use the string literal or variable directly.
Note: Unlike Java's `new String(str)`, Kotlin's `kotlin.String` does not expose a `String(String)` copy constructor, so this rule primarily catches Java-interop patterns where the Java constructor is invoked explicitly (e.g. via reflection or a helper that calls `java.lang.String(String)`).
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/performance.xml/StringInstantiation

rule.name: StringToString
rule.message: Avoid calling toString() on a String; it returns the same object.
rule.description:
Calling `toString()` on a `String` is a no-op; the same `String` instance is returned. Remove the unnecessary call.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/performance.xml/StringToString

rule.name: TooFewBranchesForWhenExpression
rule.message: A when expression with too few branches can be replaced with a simpler if/else.
rule.description:
A condition-only `when` expression (no subject) with very few branches carries more syntax overhead than a plain `if`/`if-else`. Use `if` when only one or two conditions are needed.
Note: `when` expressions with a typed subject (e.g., `when (sealedValue)`) are always allowed regardless of branch count. They serve as exhaustive pattern matching on enums and sealed classes, which is idiomatic Kotlin even with only two outcomes.
Kotlin equivalent of Java rule: category/java/performance.xml/TooFewBranchesForASwitchStatement
